questions.stem: Convert the polar coordinate (5, 60°) to rectangular form.
questions.explanation: In polar coordinates, (r, θ) represents the distance r from the origin and the angle θ measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis. To convert to rectangular form (x, y), use the formulas x = rcos(θ) and y = rsin(θ).
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to confuse sine with cosine or to apply the wrong angle (e.g., using θ instead of 60°).

questions.stem: Convert the polar coordinate (3, -45°) to rectangular form.
questions.explanation: When the angle is negative, remember to adjust the cosine and sine accordingly. In this case, cos(-45°) = cos(45°) and sin(-45°) = -sin(45°).
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to forget that only the sine changes sign when the angle is negative.

questions.stem: Convert the polar coordinate (7, 210°) to rectangular form.
questions.explanation: When converting to rectangular form, consider the quadrant in which the angle lies and adjust the cosine accordingly. In this case, cos(210°) = -cos(30°).
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to forget that the cosine function changes sign when the angle moves from the first to the second or third quadrant.

questions.stem: Convert the polar coordinate (8, 270°) to rectangular form.
questions.explanation: At 270°, the angle is in the third quadrant where the cosine is negative and sine is positive. However, cos(90°) = 0, so the x-coordinate will be zero.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to forget that cos(90°) is zero.

questions.stem: Convert the polar coordinate (2, π/3) to rectangular form.  (Note: π = 3.14159...)
questions.explanation: When working with radians, remember to use the appropriate trigonometric values. In this case, cos(π/3) = 1/2 and sin(π/3) = √3/2.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to confuse sine and cosine or to apply the wrong value for π.

questions.stem: Convert the polar coordinate (4, -π/4) to rectangular form.  (Note: π = 3.14159...)
questions.explanation: When converting from radians and the angle is negative, remember to adjust the cosine accordingly. In this case, cos(-π/4) = cos(π/4).
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to forget that the cosine function changes sign when the angle moves from the first to the second or third quadrant.

questions.stem: Convert the polar coordinate (6, 5π/2) to rectangular form.  (Note: π = 3.14159...)
questions.explanation: At 5π/2 radians, the angle is in the fourth quadrant where the cosine is positive and sine is negative. However, cos(π/2) = 0, so the x-ordinate will be zero.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to forget that cos(π/2) is zero.
